figures.caption: Figure 3: rsignal (left), ∂trsignal (middle) and CSF · ∂trsignal (right) calculated using ImageNet 256 × 256 training dataset, 500 linear time values t and linear noise schedule at = t, bt = 1 − t. Frequencies are plotted in the log space. In the plots t = 0 corresponds to pure noise and t = 1 to the clean image, therefore the denoising process happens from left to right. First two plots show that the denoising process reconstructs spatial frequencies hierarchically, in a coarse-to-fine manner. In the last plot high frequency values of ∆rsignal are supressed while low and mid-range frequencies are amplified, which aligns with the CSF.

Figure 4: Resulting wCSFlow (left) and a comparison of sampling methods during inference including our weighted method (right). In the plots the denoising process happens from left to right. Our pure weights strongly bias the model towards early to mid-range generation stages. The step sizes grid resulting from interpolating our weights with uniform ones allocates smaller steps in the same time intervals as described before while increasing step sizes in the late denoising stages.

Table 1: Effect of our weighting scheme on text-to-image generation (512× 512). We compare the baseline model with its modified variants. α1 denotes interpolation parameter in finetuning and α2 in inference. Both of our modifications independently improve the baseline model and perform the best applied together.

Figure 5: Comparison of the base PixelGen-XXL/16 model (left) with our weighted version (with α1 = 0.8 and α2 = 0.7) (right) in text-to-image generation. All images are 512 × 512 resolution. We observe that with our weights, samples often yield much less cartoonish-looking generations. Best viewed zoomed in. More results can be found in the appendix.

Figure 7: Change in GenEval score across interpolation parameter α in inference for all three perception-driven methods. We interpolate with uniform (left) and shifted uniform weights (right). Our method surpasses other two when using weights directly (for α = 1.0).

Figure 8: Change in generated images for increasing α, interpolating from uniform weights α1 = α2 = 0.0 to our perception-driven weights α1 = α2 = 1.0 for two fixed seeds. We observe that images become visually more realistic when increasing α. Best viewed zoomed in.

Figure 9: Visualization of CSF (left) and CSF values for spatial frequencies in cycles/pixel domain (right). We plot CSF in log-log space on top of spatial frequencies to visualize the idea of CSF. We assume viewing distance of 40 cm and physical size of the plot 7 cm (≈ 1 3 of an A4 page).
Figure 10: Pair comparisons between PixelGen-XXL/16 and CSFlow-weighted version (ours). Image pair indices were sampled randomly.
